We also evaluate model robustness to altering the physical properties of the object, specifically friction and mass as shown in Figure 7 (middle). When friction is reduced, Hora+ControlNet(Sparsh-X) outperforms all other policy variants. By using a synergy of all tactile modes, it can maintain object stability without losing grasp. In contrast, Hora+ControlNet(image) struggles, possibly indicating that changes in the contact patch are too subtle to be captured by Sparsh-X from tactile images alone. This result underscores the complementary strengths of multisensory touch. When the object’s mass is increased, Hora+ControlNet(Sparsh-X) and Hora+ControlNet(image) allow the baseline policy to adapt its finger gaiting to compensate for the added weight. This adaptation is possible because the tactile properties of the object can be captured by Sparsh-X and transferred to the privilege information embedding in the latent space.

## 5 Discussion and Conclusion

We present Sparsh-X, a self-supervised backbone for general multisensory touch representations. Through both policy learning and supervised tactile experiments, we demonstrate that incorporating multisensory touch from Digit 360 and scale pretraining over $\sim 1M$ samples significantly enhances task performance compared to using end-to-end approaches with tactile images alone.

Our study is driven by two central research questions. First, how can real-world touch representations be leveraged for manipulation policy learning? Sparsh-X pretraining enables better and more robust policies. We explore two approaches: imitation learning (IL) and tactile adaptation of sim-trained policies. IL is naturally suited as demonstrations capture rich tactile signals from all modalities provided by Digit 360. For sim-policies, we propose tactile adaptation via ControlNet, enabling the propagation of tactile information previously accessible only in simulation as privileged information. We validate these approaches on two fundamental manipulation tasks: plug insertion and in-hand object rotation. Notably, Sparsh-X enhances policy performance by 63% over policies using tactile images alone and improves robustness by 90% by using touch to recover object state during manipulation.

Second, what tactile properties do our representations capture? We find that Sparsh-X representations effectively captures physical properties that allows to identify objects, actions, surfaces, estimate intrinsics properties and forces from multisensory touch signals. We evaluate Sparsh-X on a suite of supervised benchmark tasks common in the literature: object-action recognition, material-quantity estimation, and force prediction. We perform ablations over tactile input modalities and training data budgets to assess the impact of pretraining and multisensory fusion. Our results show that a synergy of touch from images, audio, IMU, and pressure, leads to higher accuracy across all tasks even in low-data regimes. Compared to training end-to-end with tactile images only, Sparsh-X achieves an average improvement of 48% across all tasks, demonstrating the benefits of both pretraining and touch sensory fusion.

## Limitations

While our study highlights the benefits of multisensory touch and self-supervised pretraining, some limitations remain. Each modality introduces its own challenges in capturing a broad and diverse set of contact interactions at scale. In our pretraining dataset, the tactile image modality from the Digit 360 sensor exhibits the lowest diversity in terms of number of different devices used with their own optical artifacts, potentially limiting its generalization in downstream performance. We believe that as the community increasingly adopts multisensory tactile sensors like the Digit 360, collaborative efforts can help build larger and more diverse datasets to support scalable pretraining. Additionally, our experiments focus exclusively on frozen Sparsh-X representations to understand the pure impact of pretraining on generalization. However, allowing fine-tuning with task-specific data could further improve performance and help compensate for modality-specific data limitations. Finally, our evaluation of force sensing is limited to normal force estimation under controlled contact conditions. Generalizing to varying contact geometries and multiple simultaneous contacts remains an open area for future work. Moreover, we do not consider shear force estimation in this study, as separating the effects of extrinsic forces from the internal deformation of the elastomer presents non-trivial modeling challenges.

### A.1 Dataset for Sparsh-X SSL Pretraining

*Figure 8: Distribution of recorded Digit 360 data by platform. The dataset includes 18.6 hours of data collected using two platforms: the Allegro hand (4.5 hours) and the mobile picker tool (14.1 hours).*

Our self-supervised learning (SSL) dataset is sourced from two platforms: an Allegro hand equipped with Digit 360 sensors mounted on each fingertip, and a custom mobile picker tool with sensors integrated into its gripping mechanism. Since SSL representation learning does not require labeled data, we collect tactile data by having the Allegro hand interact rummaging freely with a tray filled with LEGO blocks and marbles. This setup enables the capture of rich, multi-contact interactions with objects that feature distinctive geometries, such as spherical shapes and sharp edges.

The mobile picker is used to gather tactile data from everyday manipulation actions, including tapping and sliding, across surfaces with varying friction and stiffness. This allows us to record both intrinsic and extrinsic contact interactions. We collected eight sequences with the Allegro hand, each lasting approximately 8.5 minutes, recording data from all four fingers. From the mobile picker, we gathered 104 sequences with an average duration of 3 minutes, logging data from both sensors on the gripper. For the subset of the dataset collected with the mobile picker, we provide annotations indicating the object in grasp, the action performed, and the surface in contact, to support downstream evaluation tasks. In total (see Figure 8), our dataset spans 18.6 hours of tactile data collected from six different Digit 360 sensors.

Sparsh-X processes temporal windows of data from each tactile modality. A visualization of the input data is shown in Figure 9.

Images. We input pairs of tactile images sampled with a temporal stride of 5, concatenated along the channel dimension. These images are captured using a hyperfisheye lens in Digit 360, allowing us to view the entire dome-shaped elastomer surface. Unlike planar GelSight-like sensors, these images include reflections from the surrounding LED light sources, visible near the center of the dome. While these reflections act as useful markers, encoding meaningful information about gel deformation upon contact, they also pose challenges for standard preprocessing techniques such as background subtraction or lighting augmentations, which risk corrupting the contact signal.

Audio. Digit 360 sensor is equipped with two contact microphones that capture vibrations, sampled at 48kHz. This signal is especially informative for detecting changes in contact state, such as making and breaking contact. Sparsh-X processes 0.5sec windows of audio data from each microphone in the frequency domain. After standardization and conversion to log-mel spectrograms, the audio is treated as a single-channel image input to the model.

IMU and Pressure. We extract 0.5 second and 1 second windows of data from the 3-axis accelerometer and the static pressure sensor embedded in the Digit 360. Each window is standardized using the mean and standard deviation computed per sequence to ensure consistency across variations in sensor signal amplitude.

## Appendix B Benchmarking Sparsh-X for physical properties comprehension

*Figure 12: Confusion matrix for object-action-surface classification. We compare an end-to-end classifier trained solely on tactile images with a classifier trained on frozen Sparsh-X representations, under a 50% training data budget.*

#### Object-Action-Surface Classification.

This task evaluates whether Sparsh-X can capture tactile cues that enable the identification of objects through both intrinsic and extrinsic contact interactions. The goal is to jointly classify the object being grasped, the action performed, and the surface in contact. The selected objects and surfaces span a range of properties, including texture, hardness, and friction.

We use representations from Sparsh-X to train a downstream classifier on the dataset described in Appendix A.2. Figure 12 shows confusion matrices on the test set for two classifiers: one trained using frozen Sparsh-X representations with all tactile modalities as input, and another trained end-to-end (E2E) using only tactile images. Note that the classification task involves 36 classes, representing all combinations of object, action, and surface. The results shown in the figure correspond to training with 50% of the labeled training set.

The Sparsh-X-based classifier shows stronger diagonal alignment, indicating more accurate predictions across the 36 joint object-action-surface classes. In contrast, the E2E model suffers from greater confusion among similar classes, particularly those with overlapping surface or action components (e.g., misclassifying "Tap-Foamwork" as "Tap-Fabric" or "Slide-Plastic"). These results highlight the benefit of multimodal tactile representations: incorporating audio, motion (IMU), and pressure modalities helps disambiguate fine-grained contact dynamics that are challenging to capture with images alone.

#### Material-Quantity Estimation.

This task further evaluates Sparsh-X ’s ability to comprehend physical properties. Specifically, we focus on distinguishing materials based on their granularity and viscosity (e.g., solids and liquids), as well as estimating mass through coarse volume classification. ### C.3 In-Hand rotation with sim-to-real tactile adaption

#### Training details.

Hora [51] is a two-stage policy that rotates objects along the z-axis. The first stage trains the policy using privileged information, which includes the object’s state or pose, local shape, mass, friction, and other physical properties that can be perceived by the fingertips. The second stage trains an adaptation module to approximate the latent space of the privileged information from the discrepancy between observed proprioception history and commanded actions, which implicitly informs about contact.

Although the approximation of the privileged vector from proprioceptions transfers to the real setup, it operates with incomplete information about the object’s state. With multisensory touch sensing at the fingertip level, privileged information such as changes in object pose, slip, and friction are now accessible in real-world scenarios, albeit not directly. We can leverage Sparsh-X representations to fine-tune the real-world approximation of the privileged information embedding. ## Abstract

Learning agile robotic policies requires large-scale demonstrations, but translating abundant human motion data to robots is bottlenecked by the embodiment gap and missing dynamic information. To bridge this gap, we propose Scalable Physics-Informed DExterous Retargeting (SPIDER), a physics-based retargeting framework to transform and augment kinematic-only human demonstrations into dynamically feasible robot trajectories at scale. Our key insight is that human demonstrations should provide global task structure and objective, while a sampling-based solver can be used to find the feasible solution given the physics constraints. As a general framework, SPIDER is an efficient physics-based retargeting method that can be applied to both humanoid whole-body loco-manipulation and dexterous manipulation across $9$ humanoid/dexterous hand embodiments, $6$ datasets and $3$ simulators. By bypassing the need for policy optimization, it achieves state-of-the-art performance while being 10x faster than reinforcement learning (RL) baselines. Furthermore, SPIDER enables physics-based data augmentation—such as imposing external payloads, perturbations, and new contact patterns—to generate diverse data. We demonstrate that the retargeted motion can be executed on the robot directly open-loop or serve as feasible reference motion for efficient RL policy learning. Our pipeline enables large-scale generation of robot trajectories from human motion, and we release a dataset of 6,520 simulated demonstrations across four hands and 191 dataset-specific object identities to support future research.

## 1 Introduction

Whole-body dexterous manipulation has rapidly advanced by learning from massive internet-scale datasets (Kim et al., 2024) and human demonstrations (Team, 2025). Yet, acquiring generalizable whole-body manipulation across embodiments, from dexterous hands (Yin et al., 2025b; Zhong et al., 2025; Qi et al., 2023) to humanoid whole-body control (Li et al., 2025b; Ze et al., 2025), remains prohibitively expensive due to hardware constraints, task complexity, and lack of large-scale embodiment-specific data (Zhang et al., 2025; Xu et al., 2025). On the other hand, abundant human motion data is readily available, including large-scale motion-capture datasets (Zhan et al., 2024; Mahmood et al., 2019), internet-scale video collections (Ren et al., 2025), and VR-based interfaces (Hoque et al., 2025). Recent advances in computer vision have made it possible to reconstruct 3D human body (Goel et al., 2023) and hand motion (Pavlakos et al., 2024), as well as object meshes (Xiang et al., 2025) and trajectories (Wen et al., 2024), directly from videos. These developments create a unique opportunity to leverage human motion as a scalable source of demonstrations for learning humanoid and dexterous robot control. However, a fundamental challenge arises: the embodiment gap - the mismatch in morphology, dynamics, and actuation between humans and robots - which leads to infeasible motion during transfer. This motivates our central research question:

How can we efficiently and reliably transform human motion into feasible robot trajectories that respect dynamics and contact?

We formulate this as a physics-based retargeting problem (Reda et al., 2023): given kinematic human demonstrations, generate robot motions that (a) align the robot’s poses with human poses, (b) follow physics constraints, and (c) preserve the task objectives of the demonstrated behavior (e.g. object manipulation). The problem arises from the following challenges: (a) Flexibility and generalizability: given diverse data sources and target embodiments, the framework should work for diverse tasks and human-object interactions. (b) Scalability and efficiency: the abundance of internet-scale human data requires approaches that are both computationally efficient and scalable to large datasets. Existing methods struggle to bridge these gaps: inverse-kinematics (IK) approaches (Qin et al., 2022; Yin et al., 2025a) are efficient but dynamically infeasible; reinforcement learning (RL) approaches (Li et al., 2025c; Lum et al., 2025) are general but require expensive trajectory-specific policy optimization; teleoperation (Yin et al., 2025b) is dynamically feasible but often labor-intensive and embodiment-specific.

To achieve scalable, general, and flexible physics-based cross-embodiment retargeting, we propose Scalable Physics-Informed DExterous Retargeting (SPIDER), a sampling-based approach with contact guidance. Our key insight is that human demonstrations provide high-level guidance in terms of robot motion and task specification, while a physics simulator grounds trajectories to ensure dynamical feasibility and contact correctness through large-scale sampling. Our method lies in the middle of the trade-off between gradient-based optimization and reinforcement learning: it preserves the efficiency of optimization-based methods as a learning-free method, while achieving the generalizability of reinforcement learning as no gradient is required. The resulting framework is embodiment-agnostic and task-general: it can be applied to any robot-environment interaction as long as the scene can be simulated.

Contributions. Our contributions are summarized as follows:

- • We introduce SPIDER, a general and scalable physics-based retargeting framework that supports both dexterous manipulation and humanoid whole-body loco-manipulation across 9 diverse robot embodiments, 6 datasets, and 3 simulators. It achieves state-of-the-art performance while being $10\times$ faster than RL-based methods.

- • We demonstrate our method’s flexibility and applicability to diverse policy learning and data generation applications, including more efficient RL policy learning, data augmentation for novel physics constraints, user intent preservation with contact guidance, and trajectory robustification for direct real-robot deployment.

- • Our pipeline enables the generation of large-scale, robot-feasible datasets, with 6532 demonstrations across 4 distinct robotic hands and 191 different objects, derived from human data. We release the full data generation pipeline to assist future research.

## 2 Related Work

### 2.1 Learning Manipulation from Human Data

Recent work explores learning robot skills from large-scale human videos by first detecting actions and transferring them to robots. One common strategy is kinematic retargeting, where human poses or keypoints are mapped to robot motions, as in DemoDiffusion (Park et al., 2025), OKAMI (Li et al., 2024), R+X (Papagiannis et al., 2025), and EgoZero (Liu et al., 2025). Another strategy is to train a human-centric policy and then adapt it to robots through fine-tuning with in-domain data, as in MimicPlay (Wang et al., 2023), Track2Act (Bharadhwaj et al., 2024), and VideoDex (Shaw et al., 2022). Our approach is complementary to these pipelines. Specifically, SPIDER can serve as a drop-in replacement for the human-to-robot action transfer components, providing more accurate and contact-aware mappings for dexterous and whole-body control.

### 2.2 Retargeting from Human Data

Motion retargeting seeks to convert human data into robot trajectories that are physically consistent and executable.

Kinematic Retargeting. These methods map human motion to robot configurations (Qin et al., 2022). While efficient and easy to compute, they often rely on specialized hardware (Xu et al., 2025), handcrafted motion primitives (Wu et al., 2024), and struggle with realism in contact-rich tasks (Qin et al., 2023). Being kinematic only, the generated motions are not compliant with physics constraints.

Learning-Based Retargeting Networks. Neural mapping approaches train networks to convert human motions into robot motions (Park et al., 2025; Yin et al., 2025b). Such models can outperform direct kinematic mappings and retain fast inference, but they require extensive pretraining and may fail when facing out-of-distribution motions or novel embodiments.

Optimization-Based Retargeting. Optimization-based approaches explicitly incorporate physics and contact constraints to ensure dynamical feasibility (Reda et al., 2023). They can generate high-quality, physically plausible motions, but often depend on detailed contact data (Lakshmipathy et al., 2025), specific data pipelines (Yang et al., 2025), and strong priors (Nakaoka et al., 2005). Due to the non-convex nature of the problem, sampling-based approaches (Yang et al., 2025; Si et al., 2025) have emerged as a promising solution.

RL-Based Retargeting. RL has been used to retarget human demonstrations across embodiments (Lum et al., 2025; Li et al., 2025c). When combined with curriculum learning (Mandi et al., 2025; Liu et al., 2024), RL can produce dexterous, physically feasible robot motions. However, it typically requires training on each trajectory and significant computation, which limits scalability to internet-scale data and real-time deployment.

Existing methods trade off between efficiency (kinematics, neural networks) and physical fidelity (optimization, RL). SPIDER combines the generality of RL with the efficiency of optimization-based pipelines, making it a scalable and practical drop-in replacement for human-to-robot transfer.

### 2.3 Sampling-based Optimization for Robot Control

Sampling-based optimization methods such as the cross-entropy method (De Boer et al., 2005), evolutionary algorithms (Salimans et al., 2017), and Bayesian optimization (Frazier, 2018) are powerful tools for solving non-convex and non-smooth problems. Due to their parallelizability and flexibility, these methods have been applied to navigation (Williams et al., 2016), legged locomotion (Xue et al., 2025), and dexterous manipulation (Howell et al., 2022; Li et al., 2025a). Despite their success in contact-rich control, they can suffer from instability and solution ambiguity in trajectory sampling (Kim et al., 2022). SPIDER addresses these challenges by guiding sampling with contact information, which helps preserve the intended contact sequence. n

## 3 Physics-based Retargeting with Sampling

This section introduces our pipeline for converting human data to feasible robot trajectories, as illustrated in Figure 2. We first formulate the physics-based retargeting problem in Section 3.1, followed by its sampling-based solver design in Section 3.2. Then, we introduce different data augmentation methods in Section 3.3 for downstream applications including trajectory robustification for sim-to-real transfer, data augmentation for novel physics constraints and user intent preservation with contact guidance.

### 3.1 Physics-based Retargeting Problem

We formulate physics-based retargeting as a constrained optimization problem where a robot control sequence $u_{0:T-1}$ (e.g., joint position or torque commands) is optimized to minimize the distance to the reference trajectory $x^{\text{ref}}_{0:T}$ and the control effort. As input, a kinematic reference state sequence $x^{\text{ref}}_{t},\forall t\in\{0,\ldots,T\}$ is first provided from human demonstrations. The state $x^{\text{ref}}_{t}=\{q^{\text{ref}}_{t},v^{\text{ref}}_{t}\}$ is composed of reference generalized coordinates $q^{\text{ref}}_{t}$ and generalized velocities $v^{\text{ref}}_{t}$ . Specifically, for robots with $n_{u}$ joints, the coordinates $q^{\text{ref}}_{t}$ comprise the robot joint positions $q^{\text{ref,joint}}_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{n_{u}}$ , the robot base transformation $X^{\text{ref,base}}_{t}\in\mathrm{SE}(3)$ , and the object pose $X^{\text{ref,object}}_{t}\in\mathrm{SE}(3)$ . Physics-based retargeting is performed offline: the output is a dynamically feasible open-loop control sequence $u_{0:T-1}$ (e.g., the joint position commands used in this paper), valid under aligned initial conditions between the robot/object and the reference. Real-robot experiments demonstrate feasibility from such aligned starts. The optimization minimizes the distance to the reference trajectory and the control effort:

$$ \displaystyle\begin{split}\min_{u_{0:T-1}}J(u_{0:T-1})&=\min_{u_{0:T-1}}\|x_{T}\ominus x_{T}^{\text{ref}}\|_{Q_{T}}^{2}+\sum_{t=0}^{T-1}\left(\left\|x_{t+1}\ominus x_{t+1}^{\text{ref}}\right\|_{Q_{t}}^{2}+\|u_{t}\|_{R_{t}}^{2}\right)\end{split} \displaystyle\text{s.t.}\quad x_{t+1} \displaystyle=f(x_{t},u_{t},t)\quad\forall t\in\{0,\ldots,T-1\} \displaystyle x_{0:T} \displaystyle\in\mathcal{X},\quad u_{0:T-1}\in\mathcal{U} $$

where $x_{0:T}$ is the optimized feasible state, $x_{t+1}=f(x_{t},u_{t},t)$ is the state transition function, $\mathcal{X}$ is the state space, $\mathcal{U}$ is the control input space, and $Q_{t}$ and $R_{t}$ are the state and control input weighting matrices. Because the generalized coordinates contain poses on the $\mathrm{SE}(3)$ manifold, standard subtraction is undefined. We use the operator $\ominus$ to denote the difference in generalized coordinates, which evaluates the error between variables in Euclidean space normally, while mapping differences between $\mathrm{SE}(3)$ transformations to the local 6D tangent space using the logarithmic map. In practice, we use diagonal weighting matrices for $Q_{t}$ and $R_{t}$ , where $Q_{t}=\text{diag}(\{q_{\text{robot}},q_{\text{object}}\})$ and $R_{t}=\text{diag}(\{r_{\text{robot}},r_{\text{object}}\})$ .

### 3.2 Sampling for Physics-based Retargeting

Due to the contact-rich nature of physics-based retargeting, the optimization problem in Equation 1a is highly non-convex and often discontinuous. Sampling-based optimization (Mannor et al., 2003) provides a natural way to handle such landscapes, as it does not rely on smoothness or convexity assumptions. Intuitively, this resembles RL in that both rely on sampled trajectories from parallelized simulation to guide decision-making, but instead of updating a policy network, we directly use the samples to optimize the control sequence $U=u_{0:T-1}$ . To this end, we adopt a sampling-based optimizer with an annealed sampling kernel (Xue et al., 2025; Pan et al., 2024) as shown in Algorithm 1.

$$ \displaystyle U^{i+1} \displaystyle=U^{i}+\frac{\sum_{j=1}^{N_{W}}\exp\left(-\frac{J(U^{i}+[W]_{j})}{\lambda}\right)[W]_{j}}{\sum_{j=1}^{N_{W}}\exp\left(-\frac{J(U^{i}+[W]_{j})}{\lambda}\right)}, \displaystyle\Sigma^{i}_{h} \displaystyle=\exp\left(-\frac{N-i}{\beta_{1}N}-\frac{H-h}{\beta_{2}H}\right)I, $$

where $H$ is the planning horizon, $\lambda$ is the temperature parameter, $U^{i}$ is the solution at iteration $i$ , $i=1,\ldots,N$ is the iteration index with $N$ being the total number of iterations, $[W]_{j}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\Sigma_{0:H-1}),~j=1,\ldots,N_{W}$ are $N_{W}$ sampled Gaussian noise sequences with scheduled covariance $\Sigma_{h},h\in\{0,\ldots,H-1\}$ , and $\beta_{1},\beta_{2}\in(0,1)$ are annealing parameters controlling sampling covariance in line 6 of Algorithm 1.

In contact-rich dexterous manipulation, the feasible solution set is typically narrow, so effective optimization requires a combination of coarse search to discover feasible contact modes and fine refinement to achieve stable contact. The annealed sampling covariance in Equation 2 implements this exploration-exploitation trade-off: $\beta_{1}$ controls the rate across outer iterations (global-to-local search over optimization updates), and $\beta_{2}$ controls the rate along the prediction horizon (allocating more or less perturbation across timesteps). As the schedule progresses, the effective sampling radius transitions from broad exploration to targeted exploitation around promising trajectories. To further improve speed, we adopt an early stopping strategy (Kamat et al., 2022), where optimization halts when improvements from further sampling become small.

### 3.3 Sampling for Physics-based Data Augmentation

Apart from generating feasible robot actions, another application of physics-based retargeting is the ability to systematically augment the retargeted data for trajectory robustness, data diversity and user intent preservation.

Trajectory Robustification. To bridge the gap from reconstructed demonstrations to real hardware, trajectories must be robust against unknown or misspecified dynamics (e.g., friction, contact compliance) and reconstruction noise (e.g., object mesh estimation error, pose estimation error) that could otherwise make a nominal plan infeasible. Our approach optimizes a control sequence with a pessimistic (min–max) objective over a bounded parameter set $\mathcal{D}$ , similar to the domain randomization (DR) method (Tobin et al., 2017) but replacing expectation with worst-case cost to ensure universal feasibility:

$$ J_{\text{rob}}(U)=\max_{d\in\mathcal{D}}J(U,d), $$

where $J(U,d)$ is the cost in Equation 1a under dynamics parameter $d$ . In practice, $\mathcal{D}$ spans variations such as contact margin size, friction coefficients, and object mass. During optimization, each candidate sequence $U_{j}$ is rolled out over a mini-batch $d_{1:K}\sim\mathcal{D}$ and evaluated by $\max_{k\leq K}J(U_{j},d_{k})$ , following robust sampling-based control (Williams et al., 2018).

Geometric and Physics Augmentation. To generate diverse data, one human demonstration can be augmented into a diverse set of physically feasible actions that could be used for policy learning (Mandlekar et al., 2023). SPIDER supports generating diverse geometric variations of the objects while still grounding them with physics. For dexterous manipulation tasks, we perturb the initial object pose and scale to generate diverse interaction behaviors while the reference motion is kept the same. We can even directly replace the object mesh to generate new interaction behaviors. For instance, in Figure 4, we adapt a grasping motion for a Coke bottle to a cat toy simply by replacing the object mesh. Similarly, the same idea can be applied to human-object interaction for humanoid robot tasks. By modifying the object geometry to make it smaller and lighter, the robot can automatically adapt to the new object by lowering its body and switching to a single-hand pushing motion with less force. One can also change the terrain to transform a flat-ground running motion into a stair-climbing motion, which is challenging for kinematic-only retargeting because climbing stairs requires new contact patterns. A key advantage of physics-based retargeting is its force-awareness. By applying external forces to the robot when it is pulling a heavy object, the sampling-based solver can generate different behaviors that respond to the force. For instance, if a large force ( $120$ N and $240$ N, respectively, in Figure 4) is applied to pull the robot back, the generated trajectory will lean forward and move more slowly.

Human-preferred Contact Preservation. Due to the multimodal nature of dexterous manipulation, solution ambiguity could lead to unexpected contact behaviors that do not match the reference motion, as illustrated in Figure 5. For gradient-based optimization methods, one can specify the contact mode in dynamics constraints to enforce the desired contact mode. Inspired by this idea, we apply a virtual constraint between intended contact points on the object and robot fingers, “sticking” the object to the target configuration in early stages and gradually relaxing this constraint in a curriculum-like fashion. For the $k$ -th object-hand contact pair (e.g., handle-thumb), we define the current relative position as ${}^{\text{robot}}p_{k,t}^{\text{object}}=p^{\text{robot}}_{k,t}-p^{\text{object}}_{k,t}$ and the desired reference position as ${}^{\text{robot}}p_{k,t}^{\text{object,ref}}=p^{\text{robot,ref}}_{k,t}-p^{\text{object,ref}}_{k,t}$ . The constraint is activated when the contact indicator $c_{k,t}=1$ , which occurs when the reference relative position is within the contact threshold: $c_{k,t}=\mathbf{1}(\|{}^{\text{robot}}p_{k,t}^{\text{object,ref}}\|_{2}\leq\epsilon_{\text{contact}})$ . The constraint strength is controlled by a penalty parameter $\eta_{i}\rightarrow\infty$ when $i\rightarrow N$ :

$$ c_{k,t}\|{}^{\text{robot}}p_{k,t}^{\text{object}}-{}^{\text{robot}}p_{k,t}^{\text{object,ref}}\|_{2}^{2}\leq\eta_{i} $$

The implementation details are described in Appendix C. Compared to previous methods (Mandi et al., 2025), our formulation focuses on relative hand–object relationships instead of their absolute positions. The method requires annotations of the intended contact points and labels, which we detect automatically using the simulator’s collision detection on kinematic data.

#### 4.1.1 Dexterous Manipulation

Baselines. We compare against two RL-based physics retargeting methods, ManipTrans (Li et al., 2025c) and DexMachina (Mandi et al., 2025), and a Kinematic retargeting baseline (fingertip-based IK, kinematically feasible but dynamically infeasible). Since RL-based methods train per-trajectory policies whereas SPIDER directly optimizes control sequences, this comparison serves as a performance reference. To isolate the effect of retargeting from confounds, each comparison aligns the simulator, dataset, hand, and reward setting with the corresponding baseline: we evaluate against ManipTrans on Oakink in Isaac Gym and against DexMachina on ARCTIC in Genesis, both using the 12-DoF Inspire hand, and additionally align the nominal base controller with ManipTrans’s universal base imitator; the kinematic comparison is run in MuJoCo. Full protocol details are in Appendix B.

Metrics. We report two metrics. ADD-AUC measures object tracking quality without committing to a single success threshold: we sample keypoints on the object mesh, transform them by both the achieved and the reference object poses at every frame, and take the area under the per-frame success-rate curve as the mean keypoint distance threshold sweeps from $0$ to $10$ cm (normalized so the metric lies in $[0,100]\%$ ). Because it is computed on transformed mesh keypoints, it captures both translational and rotational error in a single number; the full definition is in Appendix A. We use ADD-AUC rather than a thresholded success rate because success is defined differently across baseline papers and neither has released a public evaluation protocol. FPS measures retargeting throughput, defined as the total number of retargeted frames divided by the total retargeting wall-clock time (higher is better).

Comparison Results. Table 1 aggregates all dexterous-hand comparisons. Against the RL-based baselines, SPIDER achieves comparable or better ADD-AUC while generating trajectories over an order of magnitude faster, since it optimizes control sequences with a parallel simulator instead of training a policy per trajectory. Against Kinematic retargeting, SPIDER more than doubles the ADD-AUC, and contact guidance (SPIDER+C, with contacts detected by MuJoCo’s contact detector) improves it further. #### 4.2.1 Dexterous Hand Policy Training

SPIDER provides an already-feasible reference motion, making the policy’s tracking problem substantially easier. We evaluate a tabletop cup-grasping task with a fixed-base 7-DoF right arm and a 22-DoF, five-fingered hand. The policy outputs 6D wrist and 22D finger target deltas at 20 Hz and is trained with PPO in 4096 parallel environments using only imitation rewards for object pose, wrist pose, finger joints, and hand landmarks. The reference comes from an in-the-wild human pouring demonstration reconstructed by the pipeline in Section 4.3. Occlusion causes the kinematic reference to let the cup drift out of the hand; SPIDER removes this artifact before training. Over seven seeds with identical hyperparameters, the SPIDER-reference policy completes the task ( $0.99\pm 0.01$ task progress), whereas the kinematic-reference policy stalls ( $0.07\pm 0.11$ ), as shown in Figure 6. Full action, observation, reward, reset, and PPO settings are given in Section A.6.

#### 4.2.2 Humanoid Policy Training

We evaluate a whole-body loco-manipulation policy that must pick up a box, transport it, and place it on the floor using the framework of Weng et al. (2025). We train PPO with body and object tracking rewards plus an action-rate penalty, while removing contact rewards and auxiliary regularizers so the comparison isolates reference-motion quality. The original kinematic motion is offset from the object and misses the grasp contact; the SPIDER version corrects the contact and provides a dynamically feasible nominal control. Under identical training settings, the kinematic-reference policy learns body tracking but fails to grasp the object, while the SPIDER-reference policy converges faster and achieves substantially better object tracking (Figure 7). Humanoid reward and termination details are provided in Section A.5.

To demonstrate the dynamical feasibility of our retargeted trajectories, we deploy SPIDER on a physical system consisting of a 7-DoF Franka Emika Panda with an Allegro hand, using the robustification method in Section 3.3. The arm is controlled using operational space control (OSC), while the hand directly executes the optimized joint actions from our method. We evaluate trajectory feasibility on four dexterous manipulation tasks—rotating a light bulb, manipulating a small spoon, playing a guitar, and unplugging a charger—each demanding precise finger coordination and showcasing the practical applicability of our retargeting approach. Representative execution sequences are shown in Figure 8. We note an inherent limitation of this open-loop execution: while the robustification and randomization in Section 3.3 make the trajectory tolerant to moderate perturbations and model mismatch, they cannot compensate for large deviations in the object’s initial position. If the object is placed significantly off from the reference initial pose, the open-loop rollout has no feedback mechanism to recover, and the execution fails; closing the loop with a learned tracking policy (e.g., Section A.5) is the natural remedy.

Using In-the-Wild Data. To demonstrate the flexibility of SPIDER for upstreaming data, we use the pipeline to convert video from a single RGB camera into executable robot trajectories. The pipeline consists of: (1) 3D mesh reconstruction with Trellis (Xiang et al., 2025), (2) hand pose estimation with HAMER (Pavlakos et al., 2024) to obtain MANO parameters, and (3) object pose tracking with FoundationPose (Wen et al., 2024) for 6D trajectories. Due to occlusion and limited resolution, the human and object motions are noisier than those in the dataset, which requires more robust physics grounding. As shown in Figure 9, we validate on single-hand manipulation tasks like pouring with a cup and installing a bolt. Real-world noise, artifacts, and penetrations are corrected through physics grounding in SPIDER, and the retargeted trajectories are directly executable on physical robots. One limitation is that, since it is an open-loop rollout, it can only handle a narrow range of initial states and disturbances. We leave the closed-loop control for future work.

### 4.5 Limitations and Common Failure Cases

SPIDER has several failure modes. (1) Perception errors: inaccurate upstream reconstruction (HAMER (Pavlakos et al., 2024), FoundationPose (Wen et al., 2024), Trellis (Xiang et al., 2025)) can introduce erroneous reference trajectories; large misalignments may cause the optimizer to converge to a semantically incorrect contact mode despite physical consistency. (2) Severe occlusion: heavy occlusion produces large temporal gaps in the reference, degrading retargeting quality; temporal consistency filtering is a promising mitigation. (3) Open-loop sensitivity: the generated trajectory is valid only near the aligned initial state—any initial pose mismatch leads to growing execution errors; closed-loop policy distillation is left as future work. (4) Contact mode ambiguity: without contact guidance, sampling may converge to an alternative valid grasp; SPIDER+C resolves most such cases at the cost of contact annotations.

## 5 Conclusion and Future Work

This paper introduces SPIDER, a general, flexible and efficient physics-based retargeting framework that enables large-scale data transfer from human data. Our framework achieves competitive performance compared to state-of-the-art methods while being an order of magnitude faster. Despite its generality, SPIDER’s performance depends on the quality of reconstructed 3D human-object interaction data; noisy meshes and motion can yield degraded trajectories. Future work includes improving the robustness of the framework to noisy data and distilling the framework output into a policy for closed-loop control.

Evaluation Metrics. In our own ablation study where we validate the effect of our annealing and contact guidance design, we report tracking performance on the robot and object motion. For object tracking error, we compute per-step averaged rotation error $E_{\text{rot}}=\frac{1}{T}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\arccos\left(2\langle q_{{\text{obj}},t},q_{{\text{obj}},t}^{\text{ref}}\rangle^{2}-1\right)$ and position error $E_{\text{pos}}=\frac{1}{T}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\|p_{{\text{obj}},t}-p_{{\text{obj}},t}^{\text{ref}}\|_{2}$ , where $T$ is the number of timesteps, $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle$ is the dot product, and $q_{{\text{obj}},t}$ and $p_{{\text{obj}},t}$ denote the object quaternion and position at timestep $t$ , respectively. We define success only on the object motion since the goal is to move the object rather than to precisely track the robot hand. Task success is defined using: (1) the rotation error $E_{\text{rot}}<0.5$ rad, and (2) the average per-step translation error $E_{\text{pos}}<0.1$ m. Since a single success threshold is sensitive to its choice, we additionally report ADD-AUC10, following the ADD-AUC protocol [Mandi et al., 2025]: we sample $512$ keypoints on the object mesh surface, transform them by both the achieved and the reference object poses at every frame, and compute the mean per-keypoint L2 distance (the classic ADD metric for rigid bodies). The metric (denoted ADD-AUC, or ADD-AUC10 to make the $10$ cm range explicit) is the area under the per-frame success-rate curve as the distance threshold sweeps from $0$ to $10$ cm, with the threshold axis normalized so the metric lies in $[0,100]\%$ (higher is better). This threshold-free metric summarizes tracking quality without committing to a single cutoff and is sensitive to both translational and rotational errors through the mesh keypoints. For humanoid locomotion, the joint tracking error, pelvis position error and pelvis orientation error are computed.

When comparing with baselines, we use the same evaluation metrics in the original papers to make a fair comparison. Specifically, we follow the same evaluation setting as ManipTrans [Li et al., 2025c] and DexMachina [Mandi et al., 2025] with their published evaluation protocol.

### A.2 Data Preprocessing

We extract a 21D keypoint representation per hand using 3D fingertip positions and 6D wrist pose from MANO. An IK solver maps these keypoints to robot-specific joint positions by minimizing $\mathcal{L}_{\text{IK}}=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\|\mathbf{p}_{i}^{\text{robot}}-\mathbf{p}_{i}^{\text{human}}\|^{2}+0.1\|\mathbf{R}_{\text{wrist}}^{\text{robot}}-\mathbf{R}_{\text{wrist}}^{\text{human}}\|_{F}^{2}$ . Trajectories are resampled at 50 Hz and low-pass filtered at 10 Hz.

### A.3 Hyperparameters and Setup

The settings below describe the retargeting comparisons; the large-scale generation campaign uses the separate recipe in Section A.4. Simulations for these comparisons run at 100 Hz physics and 50 Hz control in MuJoCo Warp (most datasets) and Genesis (ARCTIC dataset, as in DexMachina [Mandi et al., 2025]). Ablations and speed tests use RTX 4090 GPUs; the large-scale generation campaign uses L40S GPUs. All hyperparameters are listed in Table 5.

Automatic difficulty boosting. In practice, SPIDER requires little per-task hyperparameter tuning because per-step failures are handled by an automatic boosting mechanism. When the optimizer fails to reach the error tolerance at a step, the system retries from the last checkpoint with a boosted budget: each boost level doubles the number of optimization iterations and scales the sampling noise by $\sqrt{2}$ (both relative to the original configuration), and the noise-decay rate is re-derived so that the final-iteration noise still matches the configured target. If local retries are exhausted, the system reverts to an earlier checkpoint and re-optimizes that segment with the boosted budget before continuing. This acts as an automatic per-step hyperparameter adaptation: easy segments are solved cheaply with the default budget, while hard segments (e.g., contact-rich transitions) automatically receive more samples and wider exploration, so the iteration count and noise scale do not need to be tuned for the hardest step in advance.

### A.4 Large-Scale Dataset Generation

Source Data and Clip Selection. The central processing objective is to isolate the hand–object interaction interval, particularly contact establishment, and retarget the motion that forms and maintains the grasp. We preserve a short pre-contact approach for initialization; contact-focused selection therefore includes the transition into contact rather than only frames in which contact is already present. The campaign in Section 4.4 uses 499 usable right-hand DexYCB [Chao et al., 2021] demonstrations (out of 501 source folders), 169 OakInk-Image [Yang et al., 2022] sequences with the liftup intent, 441 HRDexDB [Lim et al., 2026] sequences, and 2,718 single-hand HOT3D clips. OakInk-Image is distinct from the bimanual OAKINK2 data used in the retargeting comparisons. HOT3D [Banerjee et al., 2025] clips are extracted from 424 recordings (198 Aria and 226 Quest3). Hand and object timestamps are matched within 20 ms, and Quest3 trajectories are rotated from Y-up to Z-up. A grasp event requires a fingertip within 1.5 cm of the object surface for at least five frames; lift onset requires object displacement above 2 mm per frame during contact. Clips begin 30 frames before first touch and end 10 frames after lift onset. Static grasps and clips with the carrying hand untracked in more than $20\%$ of frames are discarded. The 141 additional right-hand HOT3D bimanual clips and all left-hand clips are excluded from the reported results. Object counts are dataset-local identifiers, not globally deduplicated physical objects or semantic classes.

Representation and Lift Augmentation. Each source episode contains object poses, 21 hand landmarks in MediaPipe order, MANO vertices, and an object mesh, in metres at 30 Hz. GLB scene transforms are preserved, including HOT3D’s millimetre-to-metre scale, and the initial object is translated so its lowest mesh vertex lies on the ground. The wrist orientation is constructed from the wrist-to-middle-MCP direction and the index-to-ring-MCP direction; the five fingertip targets use landmark indices 4, 8, 12, 16, and 20. DexYCB and OakInk-Image packages include an appended synthetic lift; HOT3D packages are extended to a target height, whereas HRDexDB contains recorded lifts. The common processor further appends a lift if needed to reach 0.30 m above the initial object position, translating the hand and object together at 0.3 m/s while holding their relative configuration fixed. References are resampled to 12.5 Hz with duration-preserving interpolation and a nominal 12–64-frame range before IK. HRDexDB instead uses a fixed 24-frame recipe, yielding 20 saved reference frames after IK trimming. Trimming and resampling can reduce the final reference lift below 0.30 m. No hand-size normalization or fingertip tightening is applied.

Embodiments and Initialization. The four floating hands have six base coordinates and 16 (Allegro), 12 (XHand), 12 (Inspire), or 22 (Sharpa) finger control dimensions; Allegro has four fingers and the others have five. We generate convex object collision geometry, detect reference contacts, and construct a MuJoCo scene for each hand. Open-hand IK transitions each finger from an open pose to its reference target at its first detected contact frame. An IK rollout is rejected if it contains non-finite states, has fewer than eight frames, or places the object outside the vertical range $[-0.3,2.0]$ m. The hands are simulated without attached robot arms.

MPC Configuration. All reported runs use seed 0 and the same optimization settings in Table 6, without contact guidance or external force/torque perturbations. The campaign uses NVIDIA L40S GPUs with concurrent optimization jobs; the archived runs report a median task wall time of approximately 220 s, including preprocessing. This runtime measures generation cost, not the duration of the resulting trajectory.

For each sequence, we sample $K=512$ points $v_{j}$ uniformly by surface area on the object mesh and use the same points for all robot hands. The per-frame error is

We evaluate the fraction of frames with $d_{t}\leq\tau$ at 100 equally spaced thresholds $\tau\in[0,0.10]$ m and apply trapezoidal integration after normalizing the threshold axis to $[0,1]$ . Reported values are multiplied by 100. Surface samples use a deterministic per-sequence seed. Each trajectory contributes equally to dataset and overall averages. The main table includes all 15,041 completed single-hand rollouts, including poor reference lifts and failed grasps. The 281 rollouts containing non-finite simulated states are retained; invalid evaluated frames contribute zero threshold successes. A position-only AUC implementation, which ignores rotation, gives $63.25\%$ overall; the reported surface-point ADD-AUC is $61.48\%$ .

There are 15,302 task records: 15,041 completed rollouts, 161 IK-sanity failures, and 100 preparation failures; six further planned tasks have no record. Failures without a completed trajectory have no ADD-AUC and are excluded from its denominator. For dataset retention, we require a reference rise of at least 0.15 m, a final simulated rise of at least 0.10 m, and a final object-position error of at most 0.10 m. For this final-error test, reference positions are linearly interpolated onto the simulation timestamps, with endpoint holding beyond the reference duration. These labels are recomputed from the saved trajectories. Excluding the 437 completed rollouts with insufficient reference lift leaves 14,604 eligible rollouts with ADD-AUC $61.67\%$ ; applying the full retention filter yields the 6,520 trajectories in Table 7. ### A.5 Humanoid Policy Training

This section describes the training details for the humanoid loco-manipulation policy experiment in the main paper. We use the PPO algorithm Schulman et al. [2017] and port the implementation from Weng et al. [2025].

Rewards. We use the following rewards:

- • Body tracking reward: tracking humanoid pelvis, hand, and leg motions.

- • Object tracking reward: tracking the object motion.

- • Action rate penalty: penalizing the action rate to avoid jittering.

We remove the contact reward, self-collision penalty as well as the auxiliary contact reward proposed in the paper to evaluate the reference motion retargeting quality.

Termination. We terminate the training when the average body tracking error is greater than 10 cm and the average object tracking error is greater than 10 cm.

### A.6 Dexterous Hand Policy Training

This section describes the training details for the dexterous grasping policy experiment in the main paper. SPIDER is complementary to RL algorithms: it provides an already-feasible reference motion, so the policy only needs to track it rather than discover the behavior from scratch. The task uses a right arm ( $7$ -DoF) paired with a $22$ -DoF dexterous hand ( $5$ fingers, $29$ DoF total) grasping a cup on a table. The reference is collected from an in-the-wild human demonstration and physics-grounded with SPIDER (Section 4.3). The SPIDER nominal feedforward control is used both to initialize the policy targets and as the reference for the tracking reward; we do not use it as a residual control term, though such a variant is also possible.

Scene and simulation. The scene consists of the right arm mounted at a fixed base, the object (mesh loaded from the demonstration manifest) as a dynamic rigid body, and a table with its top surface at $0.75$ m. The environment runs at $20$ Hz control over a $120$ Hz PhysX simulation (decimation $6$ ; TGS solver with $16$ position iterations, $2$ mm contact offset), with episodes of $12$ s ( $\approx 240$ policy steps) and $4096$ parallel environments. The arm uses per-joint PD gains identified from the physical system.

Action space ( $28$ -D). The policy outputs a $28$ -D vector in $[-1,1]$ that is scaled by per-step limits and accumulated onto persistent wrist and finger targets (delta control). The $6$ -D wrist delta (position $\pm 1$ cm per step, rotation $\pm 4.5^{\circ}$ per step as axis-angle) drives a nullspace differential-IK controller with damped least squares; the $22$ -D finger delta ( $\pm 0.2$ rad per step) is sent to a joint-position controller clamped to joint limits.

Observation space ( $325$ -D). The observation concatenates: relative joint positions and velocities ( $29+29$ ), wrist pose ( $3+6$ , using $6$ -D rotation), accumulated wrist and finger targets ( $3+6+22$ ), object pose ( $3+6$ ), the reference wrist pose, finger joints, and object pose at the current reference step ( $3+6+22+3+6$ ), the goal object bounding box ( $24$ ) and goal hand landmarks in the object frame ( $51$ ), the current object bounding box ( $24$ ) and hand landmarks ( $51$ ), and the last action ( $28$ ). We use an asymmetric actor-critic: the critic additionally receives privileged information (per-joint PD gains, effort limits and armature, object mass and friction, object velocities, and the object–wrist relative pose). The policy network receives the current frame concatenated with a $4$ -step history buffer; actor and critic use $(512,256,128)$ MLPs.

Rewards. We use dense tracking rewards of the form $\exp(-s\cdot e)$ , where $e$ is the tracking error and $s$ is a per-term scale, listed in Table 8, together with a small action-magnitude penalty. The hand-landmark term tracks $17$ landmarks on the hand expressed in the object frame, which couples the hand and object motion and is given the largest weight. We remove the lifting reward and the success bonus, keeping only the imitation tracking terms so that performance reflects the quality of the reference motion, mirroring the humanoid setting.

Termination and success. An episode terminates if the object leaves the workspace (height below $0.5$ m or above $1.5$ m in the environment frame), if the wrist drifts more than $1.2$ m from the object, or if any arm joint exceeds its position limit; episodes truncate at $12$ s. An episode is counted as successful when the object is lifted at least $4$ cm above the table while the hand remains in contact (minimum hand-to-object distance below $2$ cm).

Initial-state generation via sequential IK rollout. To turn the single SPIDER-retargeted demonstration into a diverse initial-state distribution, we augment it into thousands of randomized, reachability-validated placements. For each candidate placement, the object is randomly translated on the table and rotated in yaw (uniform over the table workspace, discarding placements outside the table bounds), and the demonstrated wrist trajectory—stored in an object-centered frame—is re-expressed in the robot frame at that placement. A GPU-batched damped-least-squares IK solver then rolls the trajectory forward waypoint-by-waypoint: the first waypoint is warm-started from the nearest configuration in a precomputed table of healthy arm configurations (with a larger iteration budget of $400$ vs. $50$ for subsequent waypoints), and every later waypoint is warm-started from the previous solution. A placement is accepted only if the arm can track the entire trajectory within tolerance (wrist position error $<3$ cm, orientation error $<0.15$ rad) while keeping the proximal joints within $0.5$ rad of the healthy-configuration manifold (rejecting contorted elbow postures). Before the object is lifted, its pose follows the transformed reference; after lift-off, it is treated as rigidly attached to the wrist and its pose is recomputed from the achieved forward kinematics. Accepted placements—each carrying a complete arm, finger, and object trajectory—are further filtered by a physics rollout that verifies grasp stability before being used for training.

Reset. On reset, each environment samples a placement and a starting waypoint along its trajectory (biased toward early waypoints, with a fixed fraction starting from the beginning) and initializes the robot and object from the corresponding validated state; for early waypoints, the object position is additionally perturbed by $\pm 4$ cm in the horizontal plane with $\pm 30^{\circ}$ yaw, and joint targets receive small noise. Episode start times are desynchronized across environments so that resets do not coincide.

PPO hyperparameters. We train with PPO [Schulman et al., 2017]: adaptive learning rate initialized at $3\times 10^{-4}$ (KL-targeted at $0.016$ ), discount $\gamma=0.95$ , GAE $\lambda=0.9$ , clip $0.2$ , horizon length $16$ , minibatch size $16384$ , $5$ mini-epochs, gradient norm clipping at $1.0$ , and observation/value normalization. Each policy is trained on a single L40 GPU for roughly $3$ – $4$ hours.

### B.2 ManipTrans Retargeting Results

To match the exact setting of ManipTrans and avoid discrepancies caused by different simulators, we directly port the training environment and evaluation protocol from ManipTrans on the Oakink dataset. The following are the details of the training and evaluation protocol when comparing SPIDER with the ManipTrans RL baseline.

RL Baseline Training. We train one residual RL policy per trajectory using the ManipTrans framework on 16 randomly picked single-hand picking trajectories from the Oakink dataset. Each policy is trained for 100 epochs on a single trajectory with the Inspire dexterous hand using the same 12-DoF simulation model as in the original ManipTrans paper. The action space consists of 18-dimensional residual actions (6 wrist force/torque + 12 joint DOF positions), applied on top of a pre-trained base imitator that provides nominal actions from the current observations. We use an action smoothing factor of 0.4 as suggested in the baseline repository.

RL Evaluation. We evaluate each trained policy with 5 random seeds (0-4) to capture stochasticity. For each seed, we run 2048 rollouts across 256 parallel IsaacGym environments without early termination, deterministic initial states from the demo trajectory, and save the 256 longest rollouts to HDF5.

SPIDER Retargeting. We run SPIDER with 1024 parallel IsaacGym environments. SPIDER optimizes only the 18-dim residual actions; the base imitator provides nominal actions at each step. The action smoothing factor is 0.4, matching RL. For the reward, we use the same reward function as the RL baseline but remove the action penalty term for efficiency (since our action is smooth by interpolation). Each trajectory is run with 5 seeds. All hyperparameters are set as in Table 16.

### B.3 DexMachina Retargeting Results

We evaluate SPIDER on bimanual dexterous manipulation tasks from the ARCTIC dataset [Fan et al., 2023], using the DexMachina framework [Mandi et al., 2025] and the Genesis physics engine. We use the Inspire dexterous hand in a bimanual configuration (two hands manipulating articulated objects simultaneously). To ensure a fair comparison, SPIDER directly uses the same RL training environment and reward function as DexMachina, and all evaluation metrics are computed identically for both methods. We remove the object virtual joint curriculum from DexMachina.

RL Baseline Training. We use the DexMachina RL policy as our baseline. DexMachina trains one RL policy per ARCTIC clip using the Genesis physics engine with the Inspire hand in a bimanual configuration. The action space consists of 36 dimensions in hybrid mode: for each hand, 6 wrist force/torque dimensions (3 position + 3 rotation) and 12 finger joint position targets. The RL policy is deterministic at evaluation time; since the initial state is fixed, the RL policy produces identical rollouts across random seeds.

RL Evaluation. We evaluate the PPO policy once per task with 5 seeds and report the mean and std of the metrics.

Reward Setting. To ensure SPIDER optimizes the same objective as the RL baseline, we delegate reward computation to DexMachina’s reward function but remove the action penalty term for efficiency (since our action is smooth by interpolation).

Curriculum Learning. In SPIDER retargeting, we disable curriculum learning in DexMachina, so the object joints are always free (passive) throughout optimization. For DexMachina, we use the default curriculum learning settings where object joint stiffness and damping are annealed from high values (providing a guiding force) to zero across training iterations.

SPIDER Retargeting. We run SPIDER with 1024 parallel Genesis environments. SPIDER optimizes the full 36-dim action space (both hands’ wrist and finger actions) using sampling-based MPC. Each task is run with 5 random seeds. All hyperparameters are listed in Table 18.

## Appendix C Virtual Contact Guidance Details

Solution Ambiguity. For a retargeting method to be valid, it is also important to preserve the human-preferred contact in the demonstration. Take the stir stick manipulation in Figure 5 as an example: the robot can hold the stick either between the thumb and index finger or between the index and middle finger; both achieve the task, but the former is more natural and aligns with the human demonstration. However, due to the non-convex cost landscape of Equation 1a, there may be multiple solutions that achieve similar object motion with different contact behaviors. As a result, a sampling-based optimizer may converge to alternative contact modes, leading to implausible contact trajectories in a demonstration even when the object trajectory is reproduced.

Virtual Contact Guidance. To guide sampling towards the desired contact mode, we introduce virtual contact guidance. This guidance factor expands the feasible solution set and biases the optimization process towards the target configuration. Unlike a soft contact reward or cost - which may still fail when the desired mode is harder to sample - virtual contact guidance explicitly enlarges the basin of attraction to make it easier to sample from, as illustrated in Figure 5. Our method applies a virtual constraint between intended contact points on the object and robot fingers, “sticking” the object to the target configuration in early stages and gradually relaxing this constraint in a curriculum-like fashion. Concretely, we impose a virtual constraint that maintains the relative position between contact pairs. For the $k$ -th object-hand contact pair (e.g., handle-thumb), we define the current relative position as ${}^{\text{robot}}p_{k,t}^{\text{object}}=p^{\text{robot}}_{k,t}-p^{\text{object}}_{k,t}$ and the desired reference position as ${}^{\text{robot}}p_{k,t}^{\text{object,ref}}=p^{\text{robot,ref}}_{k,t}-p^{\text{object,ref}}_{k,t}$ . The constraint is activated when the contact indicator $c_{k,t}=1$ , which occurs when the reference relative position is within the contact threshold: $c_{k,t}=\mathbf{1}(\|{}^{\text{robot}}p_{k,t}^{\text{object,ref}}\|_{2}\leq\epsilon_{\text{contact}})$ . The constraint strength is controlled by a penalty parameter $\eta_{i}\rightarrow\infty$ when $i\rightarrow N$ :

$$ c_{k,t}\|{}^{\text{robot}}p_{k,t}^{\text{object}}-{}^{\text{robot}}p_{k,t}^{\text{object,ref}}\|_{2}^{2}\leq\eta_{i} $$

This strategy connects to prior ideas: virtual object constraint [Mandi et al., 2025] $\|p_{k,t}^{\text{object}}-p_{k,t}^{\text{object,ref}}\|_{2}^{2}\leq\eta$ , which expands feasibility around absolute object states in RL, and contact cost [Lakshmipathy et al., 2025], biasing optimization towards desired hand–object relative states. Our formulation reduces sampling complexity while preserving the intended contact sequence by maintaining relative hand–object relationships.

Robustness against imperfect reference contact. It is important to note that, in order to maintain robustness against imperfect demonstrations with noisy or unstable contact, virtual constraints should be selectively relaxed rather than enforced indiscriminately. To achieve this, we apply a contact filter that detects unstable interactions: if a contact duration is shorter than $t_{c,\text{min}}$ or if the contact point drifts more than $d_{c,\text{max}}$ during that period, the contact is classified as unstable and the corresponding virtual constraint is disabled. This implementation ensures that only reliable contacts contribute to guidance, thereby preventing noisy demonstrations from biasing the optimization process.
